quarterly_data.signal: Q4 and full-year 2025 results (IR/CFO): core FFO of $1.86 per share in the fourth quarter, up 8% year over year, and $7.39 for the full year 2025, just above the high end of the guidance range and 10% higher than 2024. Same capital cash NOI rose 8.6% year over year in Q4, driven by 8.2% growth in data center revenue; on a constant currency basis same capital cash NOI rose 4.5% in the quarter, and for the full year same capital cash NOI also grew by 4.5%. Leverage remained at 4.9 times with balance sheet liquidity of nearly $7 billion. The CEO said the company exceeded the full-year guidance laid out last February across revenue, EBITDA and core FFO per share.
quarterly_data.figure: core FFO $1.86 per share in Q4 (up 8%); $7.39 for full year 2025 (10% higher than 2024); same capital cash NOI +8.6% (4.5% constant currency); leverage 4.9 times; liquidity nearly $7 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 leasing, a top-five quarter in company history: leases signed representing $400 million of annualized rent at 100% share, or $175 million at Digital Realty share, with the Americas 65% of DLR-share bookings. The 0-1 MW plus interconnection product set posted a new record of $96 million, 7% above the previous record set in February '25 (2025 averaged $85 million a quarter), led by the 0-500 kW tranche; interconnection bookings were $18.9 million. Greater-than-1 MW signings were $78 million at DLR share, with pricing averaging over $180 per kilowatt; Manassas, Virginia was the top contributor, and hyperscalers also signed leases in Tokyo, Osaka and Paris. The CRO said the largest Q4 booking was nearly 100 megawatts, and the CEO said this was the seventh straight quarter in which the largest signing came from a different customer.
quarterly_data.figure: $400 million annualized rent (100% share) / $175 million DLR share; 0-1 MW + interconnection record $96 million; interconnection $18.9 million; >1 MW $78 million at over $180 per kilowatt; largest booking nearly 100 megawatts

quarterly_data.signal: Full-year 2025 leasing: $1.2 billion of bookings, the second consecutive year above $1 billion and nearly 70% above the average of the preceding five-year period; hyperscale leasing exceeded $800 million at 100% share. The 0-1 MW plus interconnection product set booked nearly $340 million, a full-year record 35% above 2024, with nearly 600 new logos for the second consecutive year and interconnection bookings up 22%. The CEO said the AI-related contribution within the 0-1 MW plus interconnection category was 'just over 18%, nearly 19%' for the second quarter running, and enterprise bookings were about 35% higher year over year. The CRO said enterprises increasingly want contiguous blocks above 500 kW, with emerging conversations around five megawatt blocks as inference starts to emerge; enterprise deals of one to three megawatts over the last eight quarters averaged up to $10 million, ranging from just under $2 million to $15 or $16 million. The private AI exchange platform saw early customer adoption, and management expects inference to scale in 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 bookings $1.2 billion; hyperscale leasing over $800 million; 0-1 MW + interconnection nearly $340 million (35% above 2024); nearly 600 new logos; AI share just over 18%, nearly 19%

quarterly_data.signal: Total backlog reached a record of nearly $1.4 billion at 100% share at year-end; the CFO said 'The total backlog is a better representation of the aggregate demand being captured across PlatformDigital'. At Digital Realty share the backlog was $817 million, as $209 million of commencements exceeded the $175 million of new bookings in the quarter; $634 million of leases are scheduled to commence somewhat ratably through 2026 and another $152 million in 2027 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: backlog nearly $1.4 billion (100% share) / $817 million DLR share; $634 million commencing in 2026; $152 million in 2027 and beyond

quarterly_data.signal: Development and investment (CFO/CIO): $930 million of development CapEx in the quarter, net of partner share, bringing full-year spend to $3 billion; recurring CapEx rose to $169 million in the seasonally high fourth quarter. About 90 megawatts of new capacity were delivered in Q4 (75% pre-leased) and about 135 megawatts of new projects started, taking total development to 769 megawatts under construction; the gross data center development pipeline underway stood at just over $10 billion at an 11.9% expected stabilized yield. For the full year about 289 megawatts were delivered 'even as labor and supply chains got tighter.' In Q4 the company sold a non-core Dallas facility for $33 million and acquired land near Portland, Tel Aviv and Lisbon. The CIO said acquisitions remain a key growth component: in Malaysia (Cyberjaya) Digital Realty bought the market's most well-connected asset plus adjacent land giving 10 times expansion capacity, following the Jakarta joint venture, and over the last year it acquired land parcels in Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Portland and Chicago to support its hyperscale business.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 development CapEx $930 million; 2025 spend $3 billion; 769 megawatts under construction; pipeline just over $10 billion at 11.9% yield; approximately 289 megawatts delivered in 2025

quarterly_data.signal: Initial 2026 guidance (CFO): core FFO of $7.90 to $8 per share, a midpoint representing 8% growth; total revenue and adjusted EBITDA growth of more than 10% on a normalized and constant currency basis; same capital cash NOI growth of 4% to 5% in constant currency; cash renewal spreads of 6% to 8%; power-based occupancy up another 50 to 100 basis points from the approximate 89% at year-end 2025; CapEx net of partner contributions rising to between $3.25 billion and $3.75 billion with development yields expected to remain in the double digits; and $500 million to a billion dollars of dispositions and JV capital. The CFO said the step-up in recurring CapEx partly carries over 2025 projects that did not complete and stays around 7% of revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 core FFO $7.90 to $8 per share (8% growth at midpoint); total revenue and adjusted EBITDA growth more than 10%; cash renewal spreads 6% to 8%; CapEx between $3.25 billion and $3.75 billion

capex.period: 2026 plan (net of partner contributions, as of Feb 2026)

quarterly_data.signal: Power and supply constraints (CEO/CFO/CIO): in 2025 power became 'the industry's primary constraint', and power availability and ability to execute are now 'the defining constraints' across digital infrastructure; in most core markets new supply will arrive gradually as generation and transmission upgrades continue, and hyperscalers increasingly lease from operators that can secure and deliver power capacity on a predictable schedule. Digital Realty leans on its five-gigawatt power bank. 'Data center supply remains tight, especially within our footprint'; availability across the 800 megawatts in-place Northern Virginia portfolio 'remains very limited, with strong demand queuing for the 300 megawatts of capacity we are readying for delivery in the 2027 to 2029 time frame.' The CEO said 2027 deliveries are 'pretty exceptional and sought after' with multiple customers per capacity block, 2028 should be as attractive, and the company is 'not seeing a tremendous amount of competitive unleashed capacity'; labor is 'getting challenging more challenging by the day', though every project in the 10 plus billion under construction has workforce and supply chain security. The CIO expects demand to increase two and a half to three times over the next five years against severely constrained supply (power, nimbyism, zoning). On an IT load basis, occupancy was approximately 91% (same capital) and 89% (total portfolio) at year-end, with reporting moving to power-based metrics.
quarterly_data.figure: Northern Virginia 800 megawatts in place with very limited availability; 300 megawatts for 2027 to 2029 delivery; five-gigawatt power bank; IT-load occupancy approximately 91% (same capital) / 89% (total)

quarterly_data.signal: Hyperscale demand and design (CEO/CRO): hyperscale activity was strong in Q4, especially in the Americas (Northern Virginia, Charlotte, Atlanta, Dallas), and demand is globalizing into Europe, South America and Asia. Wherever Digital Realty has large capacity blocks (Northern Virginia, Paris, Osaka, Tokyo, Atlanta, Charlotte) hyperscalers want to deploy, with conversations running over 2026 through 2028, and customers are looking further out on the horizon than six or twelve months earlier. The latest hyperscale designs mix cloud and AI inside the same building, with cooling that's 'a mixture of air and liquid', which the CEO said leads towards inference; the AI roadmap includes preinstalled liquid cooling capacity and higher density deployments. On power sourcing the CEO said the company has 'not given up on the grid' and treats behind-the-meter as a form of bridging while utilities reinforce transmission and distribution; land sites in cloud zonal markets of 200 megawatt and 100 megawatt are 'gonna continue to get bigger.'
quarterly_data.figure: hyperscale conversations over 2026 through 2028; 200 megawatt and 100 megawatt land sites

quarterly_data.signal: Funding strategy (IR/CFO): by year-end Digital Realty had closed $3.225 billion of LP equity into its inaugural closed-end hyperscale data center fund, with a final $25 million closing expected before the next call; in late December it contributed another 40% stake in the five stabilized seed assets, taking the fund stake to 80% and generating $427 million of net proceeds. About $15 billion of dry powder supports hyperscale data center development through private capital initiatives, and fee income more than doubled in 2025. Q4 financing: a EUR1.4 billion dual-tranche green Eurobond (€600 million at 3.755% due 2033 and €800 million at 4.25% due 2037), partly used to redeem $1.075 billion of 2.5% Eurobonds, a modest interest expense headwind starting in 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: $3.225 billion LP equity closed; $427 million net proceeds; approximately $15 billion dry powder; EUR1.4 billion green Eurobond

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing (CFO/CEO): Q4 renewals of $269 million at a blended 6.1% cash increase, including $175 million of colocation renewals at 4.3% and $88 million of greater-than-1 MW renewals at an 8.1% cash re-leasing spread (Northern Virginia, Chicago, Dublin); full-year 2025 cash re-leasing spreads were 6.7%, above the high end of guidance. The CEO said the company has been pushing escalators to 'call it, minimum 3%, as high as 4% or just above that, CPI linked' on renewals and new deals because racing to deliver infrastructure 'is inflationary to our cost base'; management also pointed to rising labor and build costs, saying it picks its spots, with hyperscalers in particular, which has garnered significant interest and attractive rates.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 renewals $269 million at 6.1%; >1 MW renewals $88 million at 8.1%; 2025 cash re-leasing spreads 6.7%; escalators minimum 3%, as high as 4%
